subject: Science

placeName: Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory

points.title: DNA, genes and chromosomes
points.brief: DNA is a long molecule carrying genetic instructions. A gene is a section of DNA coding for a trait, and chromosomes are tightly coiled DNA in the nucleus.

points.title: Mitosis and meiosis
points.brief: Mitosis makes two identical cells for growth and repair. Meiosis makes four gametes with half the chromosomes, each different, for sexual reproduction.

points.title: Alleles, genotype and phenotype
points.brief: Alleles are versions of a gene. The genotype is the pair of alleles an organism has, and the phenotype is the trait that shows. A dominant allele masks a recessive one.

points.title: Punnett squares
points.brief: A Punnett square crosses the parents' alleles to predict the chances of each genotype and phenotype in their offspring, such as 3 to 1 from two carriers.

points.title: Pedigrees and sex-linked traits
points.brief: A pedigree chart traces a trait through a family. Sex-linked genes sit on the X chromosome, so traits such as red-green colour blindness show more in males.

points.title: Mutations
points.brief: A mutation is a change in DNA, caused by copying errors or by radiation and some chemicals. Most have no effect, some cause disorders such as cystic fibrosis.

points.title: Natural selection
points.brief: Individuals vary, more are born than survive, and those with helpful traits survive and breed more, so the traits become common over generations.

points.title: Selection pressures and adaptation
points.brief: A selection pressure, such as a predator, disease or drought, favours some variations, as when bacteria become resistant to an antibiotic.

points.title: How new species form
points.brief: When populations are isolated, such as on islands, different pressures and mutations change them until they can no longer breed together.

points.title: Evidence for evolution
points.brief: Fossils in rock layers, similar bone structures in different animals, similar DNA, and where species are found on Earth all support evolution.

points.title: Artificial selection
points.brief: People choose which plants and animals breed to get wanted traits, as with dog breeds or high-yield wheat, showing how selection changes a population.

points.title: Stars, galaxies and the universe
points.brief: Stars group in galaxies such as the Milky Way, and the universe holds billions of galaxies. Large distances are measured in light-years.

points.title: The big bang theory
points.brief: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling since, forming atoms, stars and galaxies.

points.title: Red shift and an expanding universe
points.brief: Light from distant galaxies is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths, and Hubble found that farther galaxies move away faster, so the universe is expanding.

points.title: Cosmic microwave background radiation
points.brief: A faint glow of microwaves comes from every direction in space. It is the cooled leftover heat of the early universe, which supports the big bang theory.

points.title: Reading starlight with spectra
points.brief: Each element gives a pattern of lines in a spectrum, so the light from a star shows what it is made of and how it is moving.

points.title: Earth's energy balance
points.brief: Earth absorbs energy from the sun and radiates heat back to space. When more is kept than lost, such as when greenhouse gases rise, the planet warms.

points.title: Ocean currents and climate
points.brief: Ocean currents, driven by wind and differences in temperature and saltiness, carry heat around the globe and shape regional climates.

points.title: Evidence of climate change
points.brief: Rising air and ocean temperatures, rising sea levels, shrinking sea ice and glaciers, and species moving to cooler places show the climate is changing.

points.title: Reducing and adapting to climate change
points.brief: Mitigation cuts greenhouse gas emissions, such as with renewable energy. Adaptation prepares for changes, such as sea walls or heat-tolerant crops.

points.title: Speed, velocity and acceleration
points.brief: Speed is distance divided by time. Velocity is speed in a given direction. Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken.

points.title: Newton's first law
points.brief: An object stays at rest or keeps moving at a steady velocity unless an unbalanced force acts on it. This tendency is called inertia.

points.title: Newton's second law
points.brief: Net force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma), so a bigger force or a smaller mass gives a greater acceleration.

points.title: Newton's third law
points.brief: For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force on the other object, as a rocket pushes gas back and the gas pushes the rocket forward.

points.title: Newton's laws and car safety
points.brief: Seatbelts, airbags and crumple zones make a stop take longer, so the force on the people inside is smaller.

points.title: Groups and periods
points.brief: The periodic table orders elements by atomic number. Rows are periods and columns are groups, and elements in a group have similar properties.

points.title: Electron shells and the Bohr model
points.brief: In the Bohr model, electrons sit in shells around the nucleus, holding 2, then 8, then 8 in the first three. The outer shell decides how an element reacts.

points.title: Metals and non-metals
points.brief: Metals are usually shiny, conduct heat and electricity and can be bent, and sit to the left. Non-metals are usually dull, brittle insulators, and sit to the right.

points.title: Patterns in the groups
points.brief: Group 1 metals react strongly with water, more so down the group, and Group 18 noble gases hardly react at all because their outer shells are full.

points.title: Synthesis and decomposition
points.brief: In synthesis, simple substances join to make a more complex one, such as iron and oxygen forming rust. In decomposition, a compound breaks into simpler substances.

points.title: Displacement reactions
points.brief: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of a compound, such as zinc placed in copper sulfate solution coating with copper.

points.title: Acids, bases and neutralisation
points.brief: An acid and a base react to make a salt and water. The pH scale shows how acidic or basic a solution is, with 7 neutral.

points.title: Rates of reaction
points.brief: Higher temperature, higher concentration, more surface area and a catalyst all speed up a reaction, mostly by making particles collide more often or with more energy.

units.title: Science as a human endeavour and inquiry

points.title: How science corrects itself
points.brief: Peer review, repeated experiments and new evidence let scientists find mistakes and refine ideas, as the evidence for an expanding universe built up over decades.

points.title: Technology that drives discovery
points.brief: Radio telescopes such as the Australian SKA Pathfinder and DNA sequencing machines let scientists collect data that was impossible to gather before.

points.title: Society steering science
points.brief: Public concern, funding and ethics decide which research goes ahead, such as climate science or limits on genetic testing.

points.title: Correlation and causation
points.brief: Two things changing together is a correlation. It does not prove one causes the other, since a third factor or chance may explain it.

points.title: Sample size
points.brief: A larger sample gives more reliable results, because one unusual result has less effect on the average.

points.title: Evaluating a scientific claim
points.brief: Judge a claim by its evidence, the size and quality of the study, whether others found the same, and who funded or made it.
